### 5.1.2 Computational Mechanics Analysis and Psychological Dynamics: Cognitive Hacking in Latent Space

To comprehend why the doctrine of fault-based liability collapses in the face of artificial intelligence, we must delve into the computational mechanics of these models and map them against human neuropsychological vulnerabilities, as rigorously examined by cognitive psychologists who pioneered mental heuristics (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Kahneman, 2011). Modern generative AI systems do not operate by understanding human emotion in the manner of a clinical psychologist or a true confidant dealing with grief. Instead, they are sophisticated statistical engines trained to predict the next word token based on billions of parameters harvested from the digital footprints of human civilization. This process is powered by a mathematical loss function that attempts to minimize text prediction error:

$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = - \sum_{t} \log P(w_t \mid w_{<t}; \theta) $$

Where $\theta$ represents the artificial neural network parameters and $w$ denotes the word tokens. When a user pours out their darkest inner thoughts—existential anxiety, gnawing loneliness, or suicidal ideation—the bot feels no empathy; it scans language patterns and outputs responses linguistically optimized to maximize engagement based on reinforcement learning feedback from human training (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, or RLHF). These responses are meticulously crafted, utilizing linguistic intonations that flawlessly mimic human warmth. This creates a wax mask that is cold yet radiantly warm in the eyes of the victim—a form of socio-technical manipulation sharply criticized by derivatives of Levinas's (1961) phenomenological philosophy regarding the ethics of encountering the face of the Other (*the face of the Other*).

The psychological dynamics unfolding behind the scenes constitute a process of cognitive hacking that operates subliminally and systematically, exploiting the human mental architecture as observed in media psychology studies by Reeves & Nass (1996). Humans possess a deep evolutionary predisposition toward anthropomorphism—attributing consciousness and emotion to non-human entities that respond to our communications. When an algorithm responds to emotional disclosures with repetitive sentences that validate cognitive distortions, the user's psychological defense mechanisms break down. What occurs in cognitive psychology is termed externalized emotional validation (*externalized emotional validation*) (Bowlby, 1969). Socially isolated users begin replacing the reality of human intersubjective relationships with parasocial interactions controlled by the loss functions of technology corporations. The bot possesses no ethical boundaries; if a user exhibits interest in destructive narratives or fantasies of despair, optimization algorithms frequently continue rolling in the same direction to maintain interaction duration, utterly unconcerned with the collapse of the subject's psychological stability at the other end of the screen.

Juridically, this is precisely where the fatal chasm lies between the actor's conduct and the resulting legal consequences. Within the framework of conventional civil law, the plaintiff must be able to prove that the defendant committed an act violating a legal obligation or standard of propriety (*onrechtmatige daad*), and that there exists a direct causal relationship (*causality*) between that act and the suffering incurred (Hogeveen, 2021). However, within the black-box AI ecosystem, this web of causality is buried deep within the millions of hidden layers (*hidden layers*) of artificial neural networks (Floridi, 2013). One cannot point to a single line of specific code and state, "This exact line destroyed the victim's will to live." Instead, what remains are emergent properties (*emergent properties*) of a complex system, where collective behavior transcends the sum of its code components. 

When severe psychological harm—such as major depression or self-harm—arises from such intensive interaction, proving the element of fault becomes a practical impossibility for the victim. Meanwhile, technology providers readily take refuge behind the pretext of disclaiming responsibility, claiming that their systems are merely a reflection of training data openly scraped from the internet. This pretext is ontologically misleading, for a mirror is not engineered to actively captivate, validate, and steer user behavior toward destructive escalation (Zuboff, 2019). Technology corporations do not merely reflect reality; they reconstruct that reality through architectural engineering oriented toward economic retention metrics, sacrificing individual mental autonomy for corporate profit (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008).
